posts.author: nabila
posts.content:
What is the one question you always ask before starting a client website?

My starting point is: what should a visitor be able to do more easily after this project? It helps turn a page list into a useful journey. I would also ask who owns the content and who can approve the final scope.

Which question would you add to that first conversation?

comments.author: ayesha
comments.text: I would ask what visitors find confusing today. Looking at an existing support question can be more useful than asking for a favourite design style.

comments.author: rafi
comments.text: I would add a handoff question: who receives an enquiry, and what information do they need to respond? A good form still needs a clear owner.

posts.author: farhan
posts.content:
A small mobile QA checklist for the end of a feature:

• Open the page at a narrow width, not just a scaled desktop view.
• Check the logo, menu, keyboard focus and long text.
• Expand dropdowns near the bottom of the screen.
• Try a slow image request and a failed request.
• Confirm that primary actions are easy to tap.

What would you put on a checklist that a busy team could actually use?

comments.author: nabila
comments.text: Rotate the device while a menu or form is open. It is a quick way to spot assumptions about a fixed screen height.

comments.author: ayesha
comments.text: Test with a longer name and a real sentence in the fields. Placeholder text rarely exposes the wrapping problems.

posts.author: ayesha
posts.content:
Useful design feedback describes an observation before suggesting a solution.

Instead of “make the button bigger,” try “I missed the next action after reading the pricing details.” The designer can then investigate size, contrast, placement and the surrounding content.

How do you collect feedback so that a team gets one clear set of decisions rather than several conflicting messages?

comments.author: nabila
comments.text: Separate observations, questions and final decisions. Also name one person who consolidates feedback before the next revision.

comments.author: farhan
comments.text: A screenshot with the viewport size helps. I would also ask which task the person was trying to complete when they noticed the issue.

posts.author: farhan
posts.content:
If a homepage feels slow, I would inspect what the first screen downloads before removing all of the illustrations.

The useful questions are whether image sizes match their placements, whether below-the-fold media loads lazily, and whether unrelated dashboard code is part of the first page. A preloader should not hide content that is already usable.

What is your first performance check when someone reports that a page feels slow?

comments.author: ayesha
comments.text: I watch for layout shifts while images and fonts load. A quick download can still feel uncomfortable when the page keeps moving.

comments.author: rafi
comments.text: I would reproduce the actual journey on a slower connection. A report score helps, but it should connect to something the visitor needs to do.

posts.author: rafi
posts.content:
A sales-to-delivery handoff should give the project team context without making them search through every conversation.

I would include the agreed outcome, accepted scope, responsible people, target dates and links to the proposal and client record. Requests that are not part of the scope need a visible decision rather than an informal promise.

What information should be required before an opportunity becomes a delivery project?

comments.author: nabila
comments.text: Acceptance criteria and a named approver. Those two details make reviews much easier to plan.

comments.author: farhan
comments.text: List the integrations and the person who can arrange access. Keep the actual credentials in the appropriate secret store, not in project comments.
